context: Artificial muscles are a key enabling technology for this class of robot. Among the available actuation technologies, McKibben-style braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) combine low mass, high force-to-weight ratio, and intrinsic compliance with a force--length curve that qualitatively resembles that of skeletal muscle \citep{liang_comparative_2020, hunt_modeling_2017}. BPAs have been used in quadrupedal robots \citep{aschenbeck_design_2006, hunt_modeling_2017, scharzenberger_design_2019}, musculoskeletal humanoids \citep{asano_design_2017, hitzmann_anthropomorphic_2018}, and dexterous manipulation systems \citep{chen_realizing_2019}. However, BPAs also differ from biological muscle in important ways: their maximum tensile force occurs at resting length rather than at an optimal fiber length, their maximum contraction ratio is substantially lower than that of human muscle, and their force output is a highly nonlinear function of internal pressure, contraction, and loading state \citep{hunt_modeling_2017, sarosi_comparative_2017, liang_comparative_2020}. My experience with \qty{10}{\mm} actuators made this gap concrete: manufacturer specifications overstate the force and contraction available at the short resting lengths a leg design requires, and designs based on those specifications delivered less range of motion and joint torque than intended. Nor could the published empirical models fill in the gaps, because each is fitted to measurements at a single resting length \citep{sarosi_comparative_2017, martens_modeling_2017, hunt_modeling_2017}; none accurately predicts how force changes when a designer chooses a different actuator length. Because muscle resting length is one of the primary degrees of freedom available to the robot designer, the absence of a force model valid at arbitrary resting length blocked accurate actuator selection. Designing a biomimetic robot around BPAs therefore requires quantitative, predictive models of the actuator and of the joint torques it can produce.

context: The present work builds directly on a series of studies by me and my collaborators. In my master's project, the kinematics and dynamics of a biomimetic robot leg were matched against the Gait2392 OpenSim model, artificial muscle attachment and wrapping locations were determined for the robot legs, and MATLAB software was developed for evaluating muscle lengths, moment arms, and isometric joint torques over the full range of motion \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019, bolen_determination_2019}. That work showed that simply transplanting human muscle attachment locations onto a BPA-actuated robot does not reproduce human torque profiles; the placement optimization that closes this gap was completed during this dissertation and is summarized in Section~\ref{sec:foundation}. The rest of the platform advanced in parallel, and this dissertation builds on its hardware and demonstrations: the biomimetic four-bar knee linkage with a migrating instantaneous center of rotation, designed and validated by Steele \citep{steele_development_2017, steele_biomimetic_2018, steele_biomimetic_2018-1}, is the knee of the robot leg whose torque transmission Chapter~\ref{ch:torque} measures, and the canine-inspired quadruped platform Muscle Mutt, formerly called DoggyDeux, demonstrated antagonistic BPA pairs under synthetic nervous system control on a physical robot \citep{scharzenberger_design_2019}, extending an earlier AARL demonstration of central pattern generator control of a pneumatically actuated robot \citep{hunt_development_2017}. The humanoid leg of this dissertation carries that line forward.

Physiologically plausible models of human locomotion use the same machinery to dissect the relative contributions of reflexes and CPGs, with locomotor primitives, Ia, II, and Ib pathways, and Renshaw cells represented explicitly \citep{dirusso_investigating_2023}, and recent models address interlimb coordination under abrupt perturbations such as the sudden loss of ground support \citep{shinohara_mechanisms_2025}. How this architecture is expressed as simulable circuit models is the subject of Section~\ref{sec:bg_compneuro}; the locomotor controller developed in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} is built directly on this two-level organization.

context: Sensory feedback is not a passive correction layer but an integral part of locomotor pattern generation. Reviews of afferent control of the CPG \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998} and of muscle proprioceptive feedback and spinal networks \citep{windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022} summarize the classical picture: group Ia afferents from muscle spindles signal muscle length and velocity, group Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs signal force, and group II afferents signal length, with load-related feedback playing a role distinct from length-related feedback during locomotion \citep{dietz_significance_2000}. Removing proprioceptive feedback degrades locomotor patterns in mice \citep{akay_degradation_2014}; proprioceptive input regulates and adapts locomotor activity \citep{lam_role_2002}; and the relative contributions of proprioceptive and vestibular systems to locomotion are the subject of ongoing study \citep{akay_relative_2021, akay_sensory_2020}. Tonic central and sensory stimuli have been shown to facilitate involuntary air-stepping in humans \citep{selionov_tonic_2009}, demonstrating that simple graded stimulation of motoneuronal and rhythmic circuits can elicit stepping-like output, an experiment readily reproduced in simulation by tonic stimulation of pattern-formation and rhythm-generator populations. The proprioceptive and contact feedback channels designed in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} follow this afferent organization.

context: For robots, these biological architectures can be implemented as synthetic nervous systems (SNSs): networks of conductance-based spiking and non-spiking neurons that are small enough to run in real time yet biologically grounded enough to be compared against animal data. The approach has been pursued most persistently by the insect-biorobotics lineage of the Quinn laboratory at Case Western Reserve University and by laboratories closely connected to it, my own included. Works in this lineage span several platforms: CPG-based neural control of a pneumatically actuated dog robot \citep{hunt_development_2017}, analytically designed dynamic neural networks for human balance control \citep{hilts_dynamic_2019}, the full-muscle rat hindlimb model and its moment-arm analysis \citep{young_analyzing_2019}, the two-layer CPG neuromechanical walker built on it \citep{deng_neuromechanical_2019}, which supplies this dissertation's controller architecture, and the Muscle Mutt quadruped, a canine-inspired BPA robot designed at my laboratory, the Agile and Adaptive Robotics Laboratory (AARL) at Portland State University, for synthetic nervous system control \citep{scharzenberger_design_2019}. Related controllers from the wider neuromechanical community include sensory-entrained CPG control of bipedal walking \citep{li_bipedal_2017}, inter-leg coordination analyses in stick-insect-inspired controllers \citep{nourse_analyzing_2019}, reinforcement-reflex hybrids in insects \citep{goldsmith_investigating_2021}, and adaptive hindlimb walking controllers \citep{schilling_adaptive_2022}.

context: Neuromechanical simulation, the coupling of a musculoskeletal model to a model of the neural controller that drives it, has advanced along three partially overlapping lines. The first line embeds reflex physiology directly into the controller. The muscle-reflex walking model of \citet{geyer_musclereflex_2010} demonstrated that positive force, length, and velocity feedback around each muscle, organized with simple interlimb coordination, is sufficient to produce self-stabilizing human-like walking dynamics and realistic muscle activations without any central pattern generator. That model became the reference point for a generation of reflex-based neuromechanical controllers, including the cat hindlimb models of Section~\ref{sec:bg_compneuro} \citep{markin_afferent_2010, shevtsova_modeling_2016} and their extensions. Hybrid work makes the complementarity of the two strategies explicit: \citet{haeufle_benefit_2018} combined feed-forward muscle activations with neuronal reflex feedback in simulated human walking and found that the robustness benefit of each depends on which muscle carries it.

section: 2.10 Testing Neuromechanical Hypotheses on Robots: The Ethical Case
anchor_status: Current review start mapped to frozen source; highlight end unavailable
context: The experiments this research program is designed to enable, including deleting a muscle from a limb, blocking a sensory pathway, lesioning part of a rhythm generator, and applying tonic stimulation to spinal circuits, cannot be performed on healthy humans. Invasive intervention on the human neuromuscular system is limited to clinical populations, is tightly constrained by ethics review, and permits neither the within-subject control nor the reversibility that neuromechanical hypotheses demand. The same experiments in animals also carry real moral cost, and their justification is governed by the Three Rs framework: replacement of animal subjects with non-animal methods, reduction of the numbers required, and refinement of the remaining procedures \citep{russell_principles_1959, tannenbaum_russell_2015}. A robot that implements a validated neuromechanical hypothesis is precisely such a replacement method: every deletion, lesion, and stimulation experiment that runs on the synthetic nervous system is an experiment that does not require a living subject, and the robot population can be duplicated exactly, so that ``subjects'' are statistically identical across conditions, an experimental repeatability no breeding colony can offer. The failure modes of these experiments damage hardware, not tissue.

The same experiments in animals also carry real moral cost, and their justification is governed by the Three Rs framework: replacement of animal subjects with non-animal methods, reduction of the numbers required, and refinement of the remaining procedures \citep{russell_principles_1959, tannenbaum_russell_2015}. A robot that implements a validated neuromechanical hypothesis is precisely such a replacement method: every deletion, lesion, and stimulation experiment that runs on the synthetic nervous system is an experiment that does not require a living subject, and the robot population can be duplicated exactly, so that ``subjects'' are statistically identical across conditions, an experimental repeatability no breeding colony can offer. The failure modes of these experiments damage hardware, not tissue.

context: Existing software supplied separate parts of the solution.
